title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
hook: a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist, and he promises to look after her
carry: raksha: protecting your people is dharma

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, the night of Shiva, and a hunter who kept it by accident. Your line was Ashutosh, Shiva is quickly pleased. Today, a thread.

In August, in office lifts and school corridors across India, you'll notice something on boys' and men's wrists: bright threads, some plain red and gold, some with a big foam flower or a cartoon character on them. Some men have six or seven, up to the elbow. Each one was tied by a sister, or a cousin, or a friend who calls him brother. Ask him to take one off and he'll look at you like you asked him to throw away a letter.
screen: `THREADS ON EVERY WRIST.` → `SOME UP TO THE ELBOW.` → `EACH ONE TIED BY A SISTER.`

segments.voice: Raksha means protection. Bandhan means a tie, a binding. Raksha Bandhan: the tie of protection. The thread itself is the rakhi. The festival falls on the full moon of the month of Shravana, in the monsoon. The ritual is short. The sister prepares a small plate: a lamp, a little red powder, a few grains of rice, sweets, the rakhi. She puts a mark on her brother's forehead, waves the lamp before him, and ties the thread on his right wrist. She feeds him a sweet. He gives her a gift, and a promise: to look after her, to stand by her. The best-loved story behind it: Draupadi tore a strip from her sari to bind Krishna's bleeding finger, and Krishna promised to protect her; in that telling, when she is humiliated at the dice game and calls on him, he keeps his word. The story is widely loved, though the torn sari isn't found in the Mahabharata's text itself; it comes from the telling. Now the teaching under the thread. In Hindu thought, protecting the people bound to you isn't a favor. It's dharma, sacred duty. An old Sanskrit saying puts it in three words: dharmo rakshati rakshitah, dharma protects the one who protects it. And in Draupadi's story, even God keeps the promise. Today the festival has stretched. Sisters tie rakhis on sisters, friends on friends, and people mail them across oceans, so a duty made in one city gets worn on a wrist in another.
screen: `RAKSHA: PROTECTION. BANDHAN: A TIE.` · `A MARK, A LAMP, A THREAD, A SWEET.` · `DRAUPADI'S TORN SARI, AS IT'S TOLD.` · `DHARMO RAKSHATI RAKSHITAH.` · then, large: `RAKSHA: PROTECTING YOUR PEOPLE IS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Rest your left hand lightly around your right wrist, where a rakhi would go, and feel the pulse, or just the warmth. Bring to mind one person you're bound to protect, a sibling, a friend, a child, a neighbor. Let the promise form without words. If you pray, offer it the way Draupadi trusted Krishna; if you don't, simply hold it as a duty you've chosen.
Rakhi. The thread tied on Raksha Bandhan, the tie of protection: a sister's thread, and a brother's promise, kept as dharma.
Your line: raksha, protecting your people is dharma. Tomorrow, the butter thief. Day six hundred seventy-six, done.

howItsDone: On the full moon of Shravana, sisters perform a short aarti for their brothers, mark their foreheads, tie a rakhi on the right wrist and feed them a sweet; brothers give a gift and a promise of protection. Many families now include cousins, friends and sisters tying rakhis on sisters.
